blocks.text: 8. The に and へ particles
Lesson 8: Location, purpose and transformation - keys to the ni particle and he particle
The に Particle
こんにちは。
Today we are going to talk about the particle "に",
and in doing so we are going to level up.
What do I mean by that?
In the past seven lessons we've learned quite a lot of basic Japanese structure.
We can say quite a lot of things now if we have the vocabulary.
But everything we can say is very, very concrete.
We can talk about doing things and being things, which of course is the core of every sentence.
But we also need to have some more sophisticated concepts at our disposal.
Things like purpose and intention and transformation.
So today we're going to look at uses of the に-particle, some of which are very concrete still and some of which begin to take us into those more sophisticated areas.

【図】The slide explains に as a target marker: an arrow labeled "mover" points from "a" toward a small bullseye labeled "b" and "target". Below, a large bullseye sits above に with "Ni marks the target" printed under it, "target" in red.
Now, we've already looked at the に-particle, haven't we?
And we know that in a logical sentence it marks the ultimate target of an action.
So "(zeroが)さくらにボールをなげた" means "I threw the ball at Sakura".
【図】Chubby white-and-orange hamster-like cartoon above どうも落ち着かない ("somehow I can't settle down"); small furigana over 落 and 着. No diagram labels or arrows.
The ball is marked by を because it's the thing I actually threw.
I am marked by が whether you can see me or not,
because I am the one who did the action of throwing.

But Sakura is marked by に because she is the target of that action, 
in this case very literally.
Now, the に-particle nearly always marks a target of one kind or another.
So, if we are going somewhere or sending something somewhere or putting something somewhere, we use に for that "somewhere".
So if A is going to B, then B is marked by に.
B is the destination, the target of that going.
So if I'm going to the park, I say "(zeroが)こうえんにいく".

【図】Mover is a grey car marked が (red a, Øが beneath) above the target car marked に (red b, こうえんに beneath); B is the right locomotive marked う with いく beneath and a green note "white-car tells more about engine". Curved grey arrows link A and B to CORE, a grey arrow runs from mover car to target car, and a green arrow runs from こうえんに to いく.
If I'm going to the shops, I say "(zeroが)おみせにいく".

【図】Train diagram of a clause: A over a 'mover' car marked が with Øが / Ø-ga / I, blue arrow to a 'target' car marked に with おみせに / shops-to, green arrow to engine B marked う with いく / (will) go. Gray arcs link A—CORE—B; green note 'white-car tells more about engine'.
So the literal, physical destination or target of movement is marked by に.
However, we can also mark a subtler kind of target.
So we can say "(zeroが)おみせにたまごをかいにいく".
This means "I go to the shops to buy eggs".

【図】Train-style slide for 「Øが おみせに たまごを かいに いく」: cars が, に, を, に and engine う, captions Øが/ø-ga, おみせに/omise-ni, たまごを/tamago-wo, かいに/kai-ni, いく/iku. First car labeled “mover” with a grey arrow to the first に-car; b1/b2 cars labeled “target” with red bull’s-eye icons; grey “CORE” arc and black arc across A–B; green arrows from the b1/b2 phrases to the engine and the note “white car & white-car-pair tell more about engine.”
"おみせ" is "shop/s" – "shop" is "みせ" and we put the honorific "お" on it because we

give honor to the people who help us to have all the
lovely things that we are lucky enough to have.
"たまご" are eggs – you might, if you're old enough, remember たまごっち/Tamagotchi,
the little egg-person that you raise.
And "かい" is the い-stem of "かう" – to buy.
The い-stem is a very special stem and it can do lots of things,
and it can also just be there on its own.

【図】Hiragana chart with rows あいうえお/かきくけこ/さしすせそ/たちつてと/なにぬねの/ばびぶべぼ/まみむめも/らりるれろ; the red う-column うくすつぬぶむる and green い-column いきしちにびみり are boxed, with green arrows shifting from the う row to the い row to make the い-stem. Examples かう→かい, きく→きき, はなす→はなし, もつ→もち, しぬ→しに, とぶ→とび, のむ→のみ, とる→とり; a note labelled ichidan says to just delete る (たべる→たべ).
"かいにいく" means "[go] in order to buy, for the purpose of buying".
Now, you may be saying, "I thought that logical particles like に and が and を can only mark nouns" – and that's absolutely correct.
Because one of the things that the い-stem of a verb can do when it's on its own is turn
that verb into the equivalent noun. Note: Refer to Lesson 7.5, the い-stem, converting verbs
(It can do something else as well, but I can talk about that another day.)

【図】Train metaphor for godan stem formation: a locomotive numbered 3 labelled “kau” and a railcar labelled “kai” with a red bullseye sit above かう → かい, the final う in red and い in green, with an arrow joining them. Green text reads “i-stem of verb / on its own is noun / and can become / ni-marked / target.”
So "かい", the act of buying, is a noun.
Just as in English if we say "I like swimming",
"swimming" is a noun, swimming is a thing I like,
and if we say "I go to the shop for the purpose of buying eggs",
then that "buying" is also a noun, it's the thing we're going for.
And "かい" is just like that.
So "かい" is the thing we're going to do and it's a noun and it's marked by に.
So, you see that in this sentence we have two targets:

【図】Train slide: cars が / に / を / に then locomotive いく (engine う), with A as mover and B as core verb; Japanese øが おみせに たまごを かいに いく. A grey CORE arc connects A to B, a black arc and white arrow connect A to the b1 target, and green arrows from the note "white car & white-car-pair tell more about engine" and from かいに point to いく.
the shops – "おみせ" – is the actual physical target of our going, the place,
and buying eggs is the reason for our going, so that's the emotional target, the volitional target, a more subtle kind of target than the physical place we're going to, but still a target.
And it's possible to have two targets in the same sentence, both marked by に.
And that's exactly what we're doing here.
So に gives us the target of an action in the most literal sense and also the volitional
target, the actual aim of our action.

Now, to get back to more concrete things, 
に which marks the actual location target 
of where we're going, of where we're putting something,
can also mark the place where a person or a thing IS.
So I can say, "おみせにいく" – "I am going to the shops / I will go to the shops" – and
we can say, "おみせにいる" – "I am at the shops".

【図】Train metaphor: a gray mover car labeled が (おれが) linked by a pale blue arrow to a black target car labeled に (おみせに), with locomotive いく, modeling "(I'll) go to the shops." Below, the same train is pulled by いる for おれが おみせに いる ("I am at the shops"); red a and b label the two cars.
"こうえんにいく" – "I'll go to the park"; "こうえんにいる" -"I'm at the park".

【図】Two-row train diagram contrasts “future target (going-to destination)” and “being at = past target (arrived-at destination)”: in each, a grey が car (glossed Øが (I)) points to a に target car labelled こうえんに, followed by the locomotive いく in the top row and いる in the bottom. Red labels a and b mark mover and target cars; the sentences read “(I'll) go to the park” and “(I am) at the park.”
Now you see, this is also a target, because in order for a thing to be anywhere,
it must have gotten there at some point.
So "に" can mark not only a future target, a place where I will go to, it can also mark
a past target, a place where I went and where I still am.
And we also use this for inanimate objects: "ほんはテーブルのうえにある" –
"The book is on the table".
"うえ" is a noun, and in this case it means the "on" of the table.

"うえ" can mean "up" or "over", in this case it means "on", and it's always a noun, 
so in this case the "on of the table" is the place where the book is:

【図】Train-car diagram with a table: a は flag above ほんは; cars marked が (Øが), の (テーブルの), う (うえに), and ある (ある), with red a/b labels under the が and う cars. A CORE arc links the の, うえに, and ある cars; a gray arrow runs from the は flag to the が car, and an arrow from “The ON (うえ) of the table” points to うえ on the tabletop.
the past target of the book, to which it went and at which it now remains.
So に can also mark the place where a thing is, its past target.
に marking the target of a transformation
And the last aspect of "に" that I want to look at is that
に can also mark the target of a transformation.

【図】A red circle around "a," an arrow to "changer," and the arrow leading to a bullseye labeled "b / target." Below, a large bullseye with a red center sits above に with "Ni marks" / "the target" (target in red).
Just as if A is going to B, に marks B, the place where it's going,

if A turns into B, becomes B, then に also marks B, 
the thing it's becoming, the thing it turns into.
So if I say, "さくらはかえるになった"...

"かえる" is "frog" and "なる" is a close cousin of "ある": 
"ある" means "be"; "なる" means "become".

【図】Left side shows ある (be) and なる (be-come); right side is a train-sentence diagram where the は flag/さくらは topic label points by a gray arrow into the が car labelled a (Øが, she), and two brown CORE arcs link that car to the bullseye on the に car labelled b (かえるに, frog-to) and that bullseye to the なった locomotive. A bottom gray arrow connects a seated girl holding a green ball to a frog with a bullseye, illustrating the “become” change.
So, "さくらはかえるになった" – "Sakura became a frog / Sakura turned into a frog",
and に marks the thing she became, the thing she turned into.
Now, you may be thinking, "Mmm, how often do people turn into frogs these days?" –
and I'll grant that it isn't very often.
However, this is a very important thing to learn because
there are various more everyday things that turn into other things and also we use this form of expression much more in Japanese than we do in English.
For example, "ことし(zeroが)十八さいになる":
"ことし” is "this year", "十八さい/じゅうはっさい" is "18 years of age".
So we're saying, "This year (I) become 18". Or as given: “This year (I) 18 years old-to become”.

【図】Train-car model of a Japanese sentence with cars ことし, Ø が, 十八さいに and なる, red a under the が car and red b under the に car. A green arrow from “Relative-time car / Does not need particle / Places whole sentence in time (lesson 4)” points to ことし; a small gray arrow above the が car points right, and brown CORE arcs link the 十八さいに and なる cars. The girl's bubble reads “this year (I) become 18 years old”; a lower arrow leads to a large 18 with a bullseye.
Now in English we'd say that a little differently:
we might say, "I turn 18" or "I'll be 18",
but in Japanese we say "I will become 18 years of age".
And if the day's going to get cloudy, we might say "あとで(zeroが)くもりになる"

("くもり" is "cloudy"; "くも" is a cloud, "くもり" is the state of being cloudy, 
and both of them are nouns).

【図】Slide titled "Later it will become cloudy" notes "it" can mean today or the weather and must exist even when invisible; blue arrows from that note and from あとで point to a large "It?", and a grey arrow leads to a smiling cloud. The word-order train reads あとで, Øが, くもりに, なる, with が on the second car, に on the third, なる on the fourth, and CORE arcs linking the に car to the cloud.
We say, "くもりになる" which means "become cloudy". Or as given: “Cloudy-to become”.
In English we could say that.
We might be more likely to say "get cloudy" or something, but in Japanese
we use this "become" – "になる" – form of speech a lot of the time.
So it's an important thing to learn.
に in the case of adjectives (aka using them as adverbs)
And I should just add here than in the case of an adjective it works slightly differently.
So if we want to say "Sakura is beautiful", we say "さくらがうつくしい"
("うつくしい" means "is-beautiful"),
but if we want to say "Sakura became beautiful",
we can't use に because "うつくしい" isn't a noun.
It isn't a carriage, it's an engine, isn't it? Note: うつくしい is an adjectival/い-engine.
So what do we do?
What we do is what we discussed last week: we turn that adjective into its stem.
So we take off the い (-i) and add く(-ku). Note: The stem is うつくし, and then add く.
Note: the く is turning うつくしい into an adverb/adverbial noun. More on that in Lesson 41.

【図】Train-icon slide where さくらが and うつくしい are separate cars; a red note lists が に を へ with "only nouns can take ni (and other logical particles)," and lower left shows うつくしい→うつくしく ("regular adjective-stem," lesson 6). On the right a white arrow points right above さくらが toward the うつくしく car, red a/b label さくらが and うつくしく, and a brown CORE arc connects さくらが to なった over うつくしく, explaining さくらが うつくしく なった.

【図】YouTube comment screenshot: 'Adding く does not make an adjective into a noun, it makes it into an adverb that can take に. Technically it can be classed as a noun, but it is an adverbial noun.' with a link to youtu.be/8AXyP5GeJFg. No diagram.
And that's all we need to do.
That's how we use it: "さくらがうつくしくなった" – "Sakura became beautiful".

"なった" is the past of "なる" because "なる" is a godan verb 
(it has to be a godan verb because it doesn't end in -いる or -える, it ends in -ある).
So now we know some ways of expressing subtler concepts like intention, purpose, transformation – and we have leveled up.
The へ Particle
Before we finish, I'm just going to give you one more carriage that we haven't seen before,
and that's the へ-car. And this is very, very simple.
The particle "へ" – as you see, this is the kana へ (he),
but when we use it as a particle we just pronounce it え.
And it's a very simple particle. It's a one-trick pony.
And it duplicates one, and only one, of the uses of "に".
So when we say where we're going - "A is going to B" – we mark B with に.
We can also mark it with へ.
【図】Heading "target - but only when a is going to b" beside a bullseye icon with に in its red center, a black-and-white train drawing below, and the caption "I go to the park" etc. No arrows.
And that's the only thing へ does. As I say, it's a one-trick pony.
It can't even mark the place where something has gone to and still is.
It only ever marks the place a thing is going to. Note: a direction, more on that in 8b.
"へ" is very simple and it's good to have another particle,
another carriage, added to your arsenal, isn't it?
